title: Act IV, Scene III
focus: the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost

teacherSummary.text: In the tent, Cassius protests that Brutus condemned Lucius Pella for bribery despite his letters. Brutus accuses Cassius of an 'itching palm' and of refusing him gold to pay his legions, while insisting he himself will not raise money by vile means. They trade insults until Cassius offers Brutus his dagger and his heart; they reconcile. Brutus reveals that Portia is dead: she 'swallow'd fire.' Messala brings news that the triumvirs have killed many senators (seventy or a hundred), Cicero among them. Brutus overrules Cassius again and decides to march to Philippi: 'There is a tide in the affairs of men.' Late at night, as Lucius sleeps, Caesar's ghost appears and says Brutus will see him at Philippi.

context.history: Plutarch reports that Brutus saw a spirit before the battle, calling itself his evil genius. Portia's death is reported in two ways in the scene (Brutus tells Cassius, then appears to learn it again from Messala), which many editors think shows two versions of the scene surviving in the Folio.

significance: The quarrel exposes the gap between Brutus's ideals and the realities of war. His third bad decision (to march to Philippi) and the ghost both point to the ending. Note: this scene reports a suicide (Portia); preview with students.
discussionQuestions: Can someone stay perfectly principled while leading an army? What would it cost?
Where does conflict appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with public versus private self?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act IV, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act IV, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene III develops the idea of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene III suggests about the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses conflict in Act IV, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene III and its treatment of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Can someone stay perfectly principled while leading an army? What would it cost? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: This scene reports a death by suicide. Support is available if this is hard to read. If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are jigging, counters, niggard, itching, thunderbolts. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I’ll know his humour, when he knows his time:
What should the wars do with these jigging fools?” In this sentence it means: rhyming in a silly, sing-song way. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Julius Caesar would have known. Plutarch reports that Brutus saw a spirit before the battle, calling itself his evil genius. Portia's death is reported in two ways in the scene (Brutus tells Cassius, then appears to learn it again from Messala), which many editors think shows two versions of the scene surviving in the Folio. Why does this scene matter? The quarrel exposes the gap between Brutus's ideals and the realities of war. His third bad decision (to march to Philippi) and the ghost both point to the ending. Note: this scene reports a suicide (Portia); preview with students. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script:
Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “That you have wrong’d me doth appear in this:
You have condemn’d and noted Lucius Pella
For taking bribes here of the Sardians;
Wherein my letters, praying on his side,
Because I knew the man, were slighted off.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the quarrel, Portia's death and the ghost? When I find conflict, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for conflict.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to power, ambition and tyranny? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
